$comment: Minimum number of tests each suite must actually run, asserted by
tools/check-test-count.mjs. A green exit code is not evidence that a
suite ran. Measured on Node 24.21: `node --test test/` runs 0 real
tests and exits 1, but `node --test 'test/*.nope.ts'` runs 0 tests and
exits 0. One typo in a glob turns a whole suite into a silent green.
Raise a number here when you add tests. Do not lower one to make CI
green: a drop normally means tests stopped being discovered or stopped
existing, and both are the failure this gate is for.
## The one legitimate decrease: retiring a ledger test
packages/alc/test/known-defects.test.ts pins each open defect from the
adversarial pass (docs/alc-1-attack-report.md) with a test asserting
that the defect STILL REPRODUCES. Those tests are green while the
defect is open and go red when it is fixed, and the failure message is
the instruction: replace the characterisation test with the real
assertion it was standing in for. Defects pinned in the suite that will
own the guarantee behave the same way.
So a fix can legitimately lower this suite's count. One guarantee often
replaces several characterisation tests, and the matching KNOWN_DEFECTS
entry in packages/alc/test/fuzz/invariants.ts goes away with it. That
case was not written down here, which left the only sanctioned
decrease looking exactly like the failure above.
It is still not self-certified. To lower minTests:
1. Follow the protocol in the failing test's message and in the
known-defects.test.ts header in full. Re-measure with the
measurement that found the defect — not with the assertion
flipping. Replace the characterisation test with the guarantee,
under a title that does NOT carry the QA-<n> id. Delete the
KNOWN_DEFECTS entry. Flip the report row to `**fixed** in <sha>`
and fix the counts sentence under the table. Skip a step and the
suite goes red naming the step you skipped.
2. Re-measure the whole suite and set minTests to the count actually
observed on the committed tree. Never to a round number, never to
an estimate, and never below what ran.
3. Add a `retirements` entry below: the defect id, the commit that
fixed it, and the count before and after. An undocumented drop in
this file's history reads exactly like the bug this gate catches;
the entry is what makes the drop reviewable instead.
Any decrease that is not a ledger retirement under that protocol: find
the tests.

DOG-36 stage-A viewer core, DOG-49 stage B, DOG-68's corpus declaration, DOG-71 label state. honesty 32, journey 26, address-equality 6, real-assets 41, research 29 = 134, measured file by file on the committed tree. QA's independent oracle on DOG-38 lives in packages/atlas-qa and is deliberately NOT merged with this: the value is in the two disagreeing. Raised 51 -> 58 when DOG-35's licence verdict made BV unnamed: a frame with no name index is a different answer from a frame with no matches, and seven tests pin that -- covered:false, no borrowed index version, a distinct info notice, unclaimedFraction 0 rather than resolve()'s 1, exact millimetres still returned, BD still covered, and coverage read off the index rather than declared. Raised 58 -> 121 by DOG-49 stage B: real-assets.test.js runs the same viewer against the templates and name index the asset pipeline emits, read off disk as data and passed through the real validators. A separate file rather than more honesty.test.js cases because the subject differs -- honesty.test.js asserts what the viewer does given a template, real-assets.test.js asserts that the one template v1 ships satisfies the interface that behaviour was written against. Its precision cases state no digit count anywhere: the real body template declares maxUsefulDigits 2 where the default fixture declares 5, so every limit is read off the bound template, and one case re-runs the same address against a doctored cap of 1 to prove a literal would have failed. The 41 are binding 6, naming contract 4, the two-document join 5, precision 7, true extent 4, BV-unnamed 6, deep links 4, notice surface 5 = 41. research.test.js is the other half of stage B: the 7 journey's middle three steps -- region research, a paper revealing all its regions, comparing papers -- which stage A loaded data for and did not implement. Its subject is the rule those steps exist to protect: an anatomical filter narrows the paper LIST and never a selected paper's own mappings. Encoded structurally, so revealPaper() has no filter parameter that can remove a row, and asserted both ways round -- a paper mapped more coarsely than the selection is still found, and a cross-atlas paper's brain mapping survives a thoracic filter. The equality guard caught two real identity comparisons on addresses in the first draft of comparePapers(); onlyA/onlyB are now derived with the same overlaps() predicate `shared` is built from. Raised 121 -> 128 by DOG-68: research.test.js 22 -> 29 for the corpus declaration. This repo holds two research datasets -- the 5-paper fixture this page serves and DOG-37's curated 30-paper seed set the QA oracle reads -- and nothing in the artefact distinguished them, so a section 7 row could drive the page, find FXP-1 and report pass against invented papers. researchModel() now requires `role` to be fixture or curated and requires a fixture to carry its caveat; both fallbacks are refused rather than defaulted, because `fixture` would label the curated corpus invented and `curated` would present invented papers as literature. Two of the seven are must-pass cases in the sense seed.test.js uses: `refuses a role it does not recognise` and `refuses a fixture corpus that gives no caveat` are what stop the validator being satisfied by any string at all, and `keeps the version string and the role saying the same thing` pins the pair build.mjs refuses to emit. Raised 128 -> 134 by DOG-71, which moved label visibility out of app.js's `ui` object and into the viewer state, per atlas and in the deep link. Six tests in journey.test.js, and three of them exist because the default makes this facet easy to fake: labels default ON, so a restore that simply returned the default would pass a one-sided check. `restores labels that were ON when the view was left` is the other side of the journey's own OFF case; `carries label visibility, and only when it is not the default` pins that an unstated `labels` encodes as the default rather than as off, so a view object built before the facet existed does not read as a request to hide them; and `says what it rejected in labels=` pins the allow-list decode, because "0" is a truthy string and a truthiness decoder reads labels=0 as ON -- the one spelling a hand-written link will use. The other three are the per-atlas round trip through encodeView/decodeView, the assertion that toggling labels moves no other facet, and the unknown-atlas refusal.

The DOG-1 section 7 journey and the deep-link matrix (DOG-38), authored before the viewer exists. Four files: matrix integrity 14, the oracle cross-check 15, the negative control 9, the UNVERIFIED rule 11, the UI-level address-equality guard 7 = 56, measured file by file on the committed tree.

This floor is doing something slightly different from the alc one. Most of these tests do not drive a build at all -- they ask whether the matrix is still an ENUMERATION and whether the rules the harness is built on still hold. The matrix-integrity file spells out all eighteen cases DOG-38 names as literal row ids, so reorganising the case classes cannot quietly drop one; the oracle file re-derives every pinned address and flag from the library, so a template or library change reports the matrix as stale rather than letting it assert history; the negative-control file runs thirteen deliberately broken builds and requires each to be caught by the case that declares it owns it.

The suite that EXECUTES the matrix against a build is `npm run qa:journey`, and it is deliberately not in the blocking chain: with no product build to point at it would be permanently exit 2 (UNVERIFIED), and a job that is always the same colour stops being read. Task 7 (DOG-39) turns it on with --strict. Until then, the floor here is what stops the authored half silently ceasing to run -- which is the exact failure the issue was created by.

The DOG-37 research layer: the schema validator, both browse modes, the solid-colour layer computation, the trust boundary, and the curated seed set. Per-file counts on the committed tree, so a drop can be localised without bisecting: schema 33, browse 20, layers 28, trust 16, seed 18, citations 9 = 124. Raised 113 -> 124 on DOG-46, which is a correction as much as an addition: DOG-50 added citations.test.ts without moving the floor, so nine tests were running unprotected and deleting that whole file would have left this gate green. Two of the eleven are DOG-46's own, both in schema.test.ts: a partitioned dataset must say per structure which index should name it, and structureIdSources must describe the namespaces the mappings actually use. Three of those files carry a must-pass case, and the floor is only meaningful while they do. browse.test.ts has `the leak detector would catch a leak`, which builds a selection deliberately intersected with the anatomical filter and asserts the comparison used by the filter-leak test can see the difference — without it, that test would pass against an implementation that leaked. seed.test.ts has `the resolution check can fail`, which points a mapping at a structure id the index does not have and asserts it surfaces as `unknown-structure` painting nothing. layers.test.ts pins the palette's exact hexes and slot order, because the order is the colour-vision safety mechanism and re-ordering it is a measurement rather than a preference. Deleting any of those three lowers the count and removes the evidence that the gate above it can go red.
